title: Anthropic asks Claude users to share voice data for AI model training
content:
Anthropic has started asking Claude users to voluntarily share their voice conversations to help train and improve its AI models.
The new prompt appears when using Claude's voice features and explicitly asks users to allow Anthropic to use their voice data for AI training.
"Allow us to use your voice data to improve our AI models," Anthropic notes in the prompt.
"Audio recordings and voice chat data help improve how Anthropic AI models understand and respond to speech. Turn this off or delete this data anytime in settings."
The good news is that this appears to be entirely optional. You can either select Allow or Not now, and there's also a dedicated toggle inside Claude's Privacy settings.
Interestingly, voice training is separate from Anthropic's existing option to use your chats and coding sessions for model training.
That means you could allow Anthropic to train on your voice conversations while keeping regular chats and Claude Code sessions excluded, or the other way around.
Claude gets a separate voice data training toggle
Inside Settings > Privacy, Anthropic describes the option as "Allow us to use your voice data."
"For approved sessions, allow the use of your audio recordings and voice chat data to improve Anthropic AI models," the setting explains.
In the interface we've seen, the setting is disabled by default, so Anthropic isn't automatically opting users into sharing their voice recordings.
You can also turn the option off later, and Anthropic says users can delete the voice data from settings if they change their mind.

report.summary: Anthropic now asks Claude users to optionally share voice recordings to train its AI models, with a separate, off-by-default privacy toggle.
report.background: Voice-enabled AI is becoming a major front in the assistant race, but building accurate speech recognition and voice response requires large, diverse audio datasets. Companies have traditionally collected such data from users, often raising privacy and consent concerns amid tightening regulation like the EU AI Act and growing scrutiny of biometric and voice data. Anthropic already lets users control whether chats and Claude Code sessions are used for training; the new voice-data prompt extends that model to audio. The article reports the option is voluntary and separate from text-training controls, reflecting a broader industry shift toward granular consent, user deletion rights, and privacy-by-default design as AI firms compete for voice capabilities without eroding trust.
key_points: Claude's voice features now show a prompt asking users to allow Anthropic to use voice data for AI model improvement, with Allow and Not now choices.
A separate Privacy setting, 'Allow us to use your voice data,' controls audio recordings and voice chats independently from chat and coding-session training.
The voice-data training toggle is disabled by default, so users are not automatically opted in to sharing voice recordings.
Users can turn the setting off later and delete their voice data from settings if they change their mind.
Anthropic says the data helps its models better understand and respond to speech, but sharing remains optional and revocable.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic's move signals that granular, opt-in consent and separate data controls are becoming expected features, not optional extras. It could pressure rivals to offer equally clear voice-data settings and deletion tools, especially as regulators focus on audio and biometric privacy. For developers, it highlights the need to design consent flows, separate training toggles, and data-deletion APIs for multimodal data. For regular users, it offers more control but also a reminder to review privacy settings; voice recordings can reveal identity, emotion, and background sounds, so sharing them should be a deliberate choice. Voice assistants may improve faster with opt-in data, but trust will depend on transparency.
report.tools: To follow up, check Claude's voice mode and Settings > Privacy toggle to manage voice-data sharing. For open alternatives, explore Mozilla Common Voice for consented speech datasets, OpenAI Whisper for local transcription, Hugging Face Audio Datasets for speech corpora, and open voice projects like Coqui TTS or OpenVoice for experimentation. These tools help developers and privacy-conscious users study or build voice AI without relying solely on closed vendor data.
